claims.statement: Evaluation has three distinct run-selection paths: a new callable target creates prediction runs, Python can rescore runs from one existing experiment without predicting, and comparative evaluation scores corresponding runs from multiple existing experiments.

New-target evaluation resolves dataset names, dataset IDs, and supplied example iterables, expands examples by `num_repetitions`, creates an experiment tied to the reference dataset, and finalizes it with dataset version and split metadata.
Each new-target prediction is traced under the experiment and associated with its reference example and example version, which supplies the join between runs and dataset examples.

Python supports non-uploaded new-target evaluation by omitting remote experiment creation and feedback uploads while retaining local rows and scores; `upload_results=False` is rejected for existing and comparative targets.

Concurrency zero means sequential execution; Python pipelines work with context-aware thread or async scheduling, while JavaScript can use separate target and evaluator queues when both specific limits are supplied or one shared queue otherwise.
Prediction and row evaluation are interleaved so completed predictions can be scored before slower predictions finish; JavaScript restores dataset order before final rows and summary evaluation.

Plain evaluator functions are adapted to the `RunEvaluator` interface, their one-or-many result forms are normalized, and evaluator traces supply source run IDs that connect feedback to its generating computation.
Row evaluators create feedback against target runs, while summary evaluators run after collecting all aligned runs/examples and create project-level feedback with no target run ID.

Ordinary evaluator failures are isolated per evaluator: both SDKs log and continue, Python additionally emits keyed error feedback when feedback keys can be inferred, and JavaScript leaves the failed evaluator result absent.

Existing-experiment evaluation loads the experiment's runs and reloads examples from its reference dataset at the stored dataset version; nested loading reconstructs child-run trees while returning roots for scoring.

Comparative evaluation requires multiple experiments on the same reference dataset and at least one comparator, intersects runs by reference example, optionally randomizes run order, creates a comparative experiment, and uploads per-run scores linked to it.

Python rejects path-incompatible options for existing and comparative targets, requires data for new callable targets, rejects simultaneous `experiment` and `experiment_prefix`, and does not support comparative evaluation through `aevaluate`.

Target exceptions are logged per item; Python's `error_handling='log'` associates failed traces with the example while `'ignore'` associates only successful traces, and JavaScript raises if the trace wrapper failed to create any run and attempts project finalization even after prediction failure.

Python provides caller-visible streaming when `blocking=False` through a background thread or async processing task, whereas JavaScript's `evaluate` currently consumes and orders every row, computes summaries, and flushes pending trace batches before resolving its iterable result.
Comparative evaluator errors fail the aggregate comparative call rather than being isolated like ordinary row evaluator errors.

For ordinary evaluation, `disableEvaluatorTracing` / `disable_evaluator_tracing` suppresses row and summary evaluator traces but not evaluation or feedback creation, and removes evaluator source-run links from normal and Python synthesized-error feedback so no dangling attribution is uploaded.

With Python `upload_results=False`, evaluator tracing uses local mode and feedback/project writes are skipped; the synchronous target wrapper also uses local tracing, while the asynchronous target wrapper currently hard-enables target tracing and is not passed the upload setting.

JavaScript `evaluate` fully drains and reorders rows, computes summaries, and flushes pending trace batches before resolving; `processData` also advances the async-iterator cursor to the collected length, so the returned iterator is not a caller-visible live result stream and rows are consumed from `.results`.

New-target experiment finalization is owned by prediction-stream exhaustion rather than summary evaluators: dataset version and split metadata are written when prediction processing ends, before aggregate scoring consumes all collected rows.
